$comment: Pins the engine template EVERY release export must be built from (restructure item 29, G10).
Widened 2026-07-31 from 'the Windows release export': all four presets in export_presets.cfg now point
at a template pinned here, so no platform can fall back to whatever stock template the exporting
machine happens to have installed. THROUGH vortex1 only the Windows template differed from stock in
BEHAVIOUR and the others were pinned for PROVENANCE alone. That changed at vortex2 (2026-08-04): the
etcpak un-gate and cvtt_export_templates=yes are cross-platform, so EVERY template now differs from
stock in texture-compression capability, and only the mouse-input backport is still Windows-only. See
each platform's 'patched' flag and $comment. Provenance is still the weaker property the non-Windows
pins also buy - a known build from known inputs whose hash we can check - and it is what makes 'which
engine is this Linux server running' an answerable question.
Three jobs, because the failure they guard has three ends:
'patches' pins the SOURCE — the patch files on disk, by sha256, so a silent edit to a patch is
caught before anyone rebuilds a template from it.
'template.platforms' pins the INPUT — the published template artifact by sha256 AND by FORM,
checked when it is fetched and again before an export (--preset-config), which is what catches an
emptied or re-pointed custom_template/release.
'binary_markers' pins the RESULT — byte sequences that must (or must not) appear in the exported
game binary, which is the only check that speaks to what actually shipped. It can only
discriminate patched-vs-stock where a patch exists to discriminate on, i.e. Windows; see the
binary_markers comment below, which is deliberately explicit about what the other presets do NOT
prove.
Verify with tools/verify-engine-template.py; see tools/engine-patches/README.md for the rebuild recipe.

engine.scons: platform=windows target=template_release arch=x86_64 module_mono_enabled=yes cvtt_export_templates=yes d3d12=no

$comment: Hash is over the LF form. .gitattributes pins *.patch to eol=lf precisely so this value is
the same on Windows and on the Linux runner — without that rule the file checks out CRLF
under core.autocrlf and this hash fails on whichever platform did not write it.

patches.upstream: none - deliberate deviation: upstream considers runtime VRAM-compression encode an editor feature (etcpak register_types.cpp TOOLS_ENABLED); this game compresses at load time (gl_texturecompression)
patches.drop_at_engine: never (re-evaluate on engine upgrades: re-check the guard is still present upstream)
$comment: Removes the TOOLS_ENABLED guard around the etcpak encoder registrations + declarations
(register_types.cpp, image_compress_etcpak.h/.cpp). The encode kernels (thirdparty
ProcessDxtc/ProcessRGB) were ALWAYS compiled into templates; only the entry points were
stripped. cvtt/BPTC needs no patch (registers unconditionally).
Presets that deliberately run on the STOCK export template, each with the reason it cannot be
pinned yet. This list exists so that 'unpinned' is a declared state rather than an empty field
nobody notices - verify-engine-template.py --audit-presets requires every preset in
export_presets.cfg to be either pinned in template.platforms[].presets or named here, so a preset
added later cannot end up checked by nothing at all. An entry here is reported as a KNOWN GAP,
loudly, and never counts as verified.
Emptying this object is the goal. Adding to it needs a reason that survives being read out loud.

macos-client.reason: The published macOS template asset is a raw Mach-O fat binary, and Godot's macOS exporter requires the macos.zip form (a zip with macos_template.app/ inside). Pointing the preset at the published asset does not fall back to stock - it aborts the export outright, which on a continue-on-error job means the macOS build vanishes from the release without failing it.
macos-client.blocked_on: Republish the macOS template in macos.zip form: take the official Godot 4.6.3 mono macos.zip and swap macos_template.app/Contents/MacOS/godot_macos_release.universal for our lipo output, then re-pin filename/sha256/template_form here and set presets to ['macos-client'].
macos-client.exposure: Provenance only. The patch set touches platform/windows/ exclusively, so the stock macOS template is exactly what a pinned one would have been in behaviour - no backport is lost. What is lost is the ability to say which template a macOS build used.

$comment: REQUIRED markers exist for windows-client ONLY, and that is a fact about the patch set rather than
an unfinished job. The patch set touches platform/windows/ exclusively, so the Linux and macOS
templates published at this tag are built from stock sources for their platform and are
byte-equivalent in behaviour to the official ones. There is therefore NO marker that could tell a
'patched' Linux template from a stock one, because there is no difference to find. Inventing one
would repeat the RAWINPUTHEADER mistake below in its worst form: a required marker that is absent
from a perfectly good binary.
So the non-Windows presets carry the FORBIDDEN canary and nothing else. That canary is genuinely
platform-independent - it asserts no dev material leaked into the pck - and it was previously
checked on Windows alone even though exclude_filter can regress on any preset.
What guards the pinned non-Windows presets against G10 instead is verify-engine-template.py
--preset-config: custom_template/release is non-empty, names the file this lockfile pins, that
file's sha256 matches, and its FORM is one the platform's exporter can actually open. (macos-client
is not pinned at all yet - unpinned_presets.macos-client - so for it even that does not apply, and
the tooling says so rather than implying otherwise.) Combined with Godot's HARD ABORT on a
populated-but-missing template path, that leaves only 'Godot ignored a valid path' uncovered,
versus the empty-field case which is the one that fails silently. It is a check on the INPUT, not
on what shipped. Do not let the absence of a required marker below read as 'verified' -
verify-engine-template.py prints the gap out loud.
Chosen by MEASURING all three candidates against both real templates rather than by reading the
patch, because two of the three do not discriminate:
GetRawInputBuffer  stock 0  patched 1   <- the only usable marker
GetRawInputData    stock 2  patched 1   <- present in BOTH; the backport REPLACES per-message
calls with the buffered path, so the count falls.
A presence check here passes on a stock build.
RAWINPUTHEADER     stock 0  patched 0   <- a struct type name; compile-time only, never in the
binary. A presence check here fails on a GOOD build.
Both wrong choices are silent in the direction that matters, which is why this list is short.
forbidden is a CONTAMINATION CANARY, and it exists because the required-marker check defeated itself.
Godot's export was baking tools/ into the game pck, and this very lockfile contains the literal string
'GetRawInputBuffer' several times over. So an exported binary contained the marker whether or not the
PATCHED TEMPLATE was used - the count went 1x -> 3x purely from shipped text - and a stock-template
export would have passed the check.
Fixed primarily by excluding dev material (tools/, planning/, tests/, docs/, ci/, .github/) from the
export, which a shipped game pck has no business carrying anyway. This canary is the belt: if anything
ever re-includes this file in a build, the check fails LOUDLY instead of silently becoming a tautology.
No required marker, and none is possible: the patch set does not touch platform/linuxbsd/, so a
patched and a stock Linux template contain the same engine code. This entry exists so the
contamination canary runs here too, and so a reader finds a stated reason rather than a gap.
Same as linux-client - same template file, and the mouse backport is doubly irrelevant to a
headless server. Pinned anyway so 'which engine is this server running' has an answer; see the
linux-dedicated note in export_presets.cfg for why an unpinned preset was judged the worse option.
No required marker, for the same reason as linux-client, and doubly so while this preset exports
from the STOCK template (unpinned_presets.macos-client). The canary is still worth running: it is
about dev material in the pck, which is a property of exclude_filter, not of the template.
Note the binary lives INSIDE the bundle at VortexArena.app/Contents/MacOS/ -
verify-engine-template.py resolves a .app path to it rather than reading the directory, because a
check pointed at a path that cannot exist would fail for the wrong reason and teach everyone to
ignore it.
Published 2026-07-30 as a PRERELEASE at tag engine-4.6.3-stable-vortex2. Prerelease is load-bearing, not tidiness:
GitHub resolves releases/latest to the newest non-prerelease, and the launcher's primary update feed
is /releases/latest/download/latest.json. A full release here would 404 that manifest and drop every
client onto the unauthenticated API at 60 req/hr, quietly.
ONLY the windows template differs from stock. The patch set touches platform/windows/ exclusively, so
linux and macos carry none of it and are stock-equivalent in behaviour; they are pinned here for
provenance - a template built from known inputs whose hash we can verify - not because they fix
anything. macos is universal (arm64 + x86_64 lipo'd); a single-arch macOS template would refuse to
run on half the Mac fleet, which no marker check can see.
As of 2026-07-31 the windows and linux templates are consumed by three of the four presets, so
'patched: false' means 'carries no patch', NOT 'unused'. macos is published and pinned but consumed
by nothing yet - see its own comment and unpinned_presets.macos-client. The 'presets' list is what
verify-engine-template.py reads to tell a preset it knows has no markers from a preset name someone
typo'd - the first must not fail the build, the second must not read as verified. Keep it in step
with export_presets.cfg; --audit-presets fails if they drift.
sha256 means THIS EXACT PUBLISHED ARTIFACT, which is what a fetcher needs to verify a download. It is
NOT a reproducibility claim: Godot does not build reproducibly across toolchain versions, so
rebuilding from these same pinned inputs yields a different hash and that must not be read as
tampering. Measured: the first CI windows build and the dev-box build had identical CONFIGURATION and
different bytes. The reproducible pin is patches[] + engine.upstream_tag; binary_markers is what
proves the RESULT carries them.
Every hash below was verified by downloading the published asset and hashing it, not taken from the
API - the value that causes a hard failure should be checked against what a fetcher actually gets.
'template_form' is what Godot's exporter for that platform will actually OPEN, and it is pinned
because a sha256 cannot see it. The Windows and Linux exporters take the template binary directly
(EditorExportPlatformPC copies it and appends the pck), so those are a raw PE and a raw ELF. The
macOS exporter does NOT: it calls unzOpen2() on custom_template/release and reads entries under
'macos_template.app/', i.e. it requires the macos.zip-shaped archive, not a Mach-O. Verified against
the 4.6.3 editor binary, which carries the strings 'macos.zip', 'macos_template.app/' and
'Could not find template app to export: "%s".' next to each other in export_plugin.cpp order.
This distinction is not academic - see unpinned_presets.macos-client.
vortex2 (2026-08-04): mouse-input backport + the etcpak un-gate + cvtt_export_templates=yes.
This is the artifact of workflow run 30866027088, PUBLISHED FROM THAT RUN rather than rebuilt —
deliberately, because Godot does not build reproducibly (see the template $comment) so a rebuild
would have published bytes nobody measured, which is the exact gate vortex2 existed to satisfy.
WHAT IT FIXES. On vortex1 gl_texturecompression was a silent no-op in every release export: BOTH
encoder entry points were absent — _image_compress_bc_func (etcpak, TOOLS_ENABLED upstream) and
_image_compress_bptc_func (cvtt, excluded from template builds unless cvtt_export_templates=yes,
modules/cvtt/config.py). 148acefd added the patch and the flag but did NOT rebuild this artifact,
so the pinned binary predated both and the ~3.4 GB -> ~1.6 GB VRAM win was never shipped.
ci.sh's smoke structurally cannot catch that: it boots the PROJECT, where the editor build
registers both encoders; only an EXPORT hits the gap.
WHY IT WAS MEASURED BEFORE PINNING. A LOCALLY built vortex2 (dev-box MSVC) was rejected on
2026-08-02: ~25% slower across every CPU bucket than CI-built vortex1 on identical code and flags
(catharsis p50 4.06 -> 5.46/6.17 ms; the features-OFF control is what convicted the template
rather than the feature — perf-deep-dive-2026-08-02.md 5c). So this one is built on the same
runner that produced vortex1, and the same features-off control was re-run against it.
MEASURED (RTX 3080 dev box, interleaved A/B, catharsis demo, 90 s cells, 3 cells/arm, 2026-08-04):
both arms compression OFF — isolates CODEGEN, the thing that killed the local build:
vortex2  p50 3.35  p95 5.04  p99 7.41  avg 252.0 fps  1%low 135.0   (better in every bucket)
VRAM, in-session census, 527 resident textures in all three runs:
vortex1 2381 MB · vortex2+compression 486 MB · vortex2 compression-off 2381 MB (control)
'compression: mode 1, s3tc yes, ok 292, bc7-fallback 0, failed 0' — real S3TC at 4 bpp, not
the 8 bpp BC7 fallback, which is why this beats the earlier 2378 -> 805 MB estimate.
KNOWN COST, OPEN AT PIN TIME. With compression ON the TAIL regresses vs vortex1: p99 +14%,
1% lows -12%, as load-time compression work lands in stream.build ASSET-BUILD hitches. That is
the FEATURE's cost, not this template's — the compression-off control above is better than
vortex1 in every bucket. Under investigation; if it proves unfixable the lever is
gl_texturecompression's default, NOT this pin. n=3 per arm: the codegen direction is consistent
across all six cells, the magnitude of the tail cost is indicative rather than established.
'patched' FLIPPED false -> true at vortex2 (2026-08-04), and it is a real change of fact rather
than bookkeeping. Through vortex1 the patch set touched platform/windows/ exclusively, so the
Linux template was stock-equivalent in behaviour and pinned for provenance alone. vortex2 adds
godot-4.6.3-etcpak-runtime-encode.patch (cross-platform: modules/etcpak) and builds with
cvtt_export_templates=yes (cross-platform: modules/cvtt), so THIS binary differs from stock in
texture-compression capability - and only that. A Linux client on vortex1 could not compress a
texture at runtime; on vortex2 it can. Note binary_markers.linux-client still carries no
REQUIRED marker: one is now possible (image_compress_etcpak / CVTT both discriminate), but
adding it is a deliberate follow-up, not something to slip in beside a re-pin.
'patched' is true from vortex2 (2026-08-04) for the same reason as linux: the etcpak un-gate and
cvtt_export_templates=yes are cross-platform, so this binary differs from stock in
texture-compression capability. It remains consumed by NOTHING (see below), so that capability
is latent until the macos.zip repackaging in unpinned_presets.macos-client happens.
'presets' is EMPTY and that is the correction of 2026-07-31, not an omission. This asset is the
raw lipo output from build-engine-template.yml - measured first bytes ca fe ba be 00 00 00 02,
a Mach-O fat binary with two architectures. Godot's macOS exporter cannot consume that: it
unzOpen2()s custom_template/release and reads 'macos_template.app/' entries out of it, so
pointing macos-client here aborts the export with 'Could not find template app to export'.
The artifact is still worth pinning and publishing - it is the input a macos.zip would be built
FROM - but nothing may point a preset at it until it is republished in macos.zip form. Tracked
in unpinned_presets.macos-client, which is what keeps that from being a fact someone has to
remember.
